title: The Three Doors of Liberation
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett shares that true understanding of Buddhist teachings lies not in intellectual comprehension, but in direct experience and embodiment. They reflect on how the Dharma is often presented as a path of healing and liberation, but ultimately reveals itself to be about embracing imperfection, letting go of ego, and cultivating intimacy with nature and the present moment. By tuning into their surroundings and allowing themselves to be present with whatever arises, one can deepen their understanding of the three doors of liberation and find freedom from attachment and expectation.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's word.*

Oh, wow.
This is great.

So I forgot to get this one off the shelf.

The first book, it's a story of five books, I guess.
I have many books on my shelf and I haven't really read all of them.
Occasionally one leaps off and talks to me and I give it overdue attention.
So last summer, right before Samish, I discovered I had this little book from Thich Nhat Hanh called *How to Love*.
I thought, huh, it's not a usual kind of Buddhist book title.
So I actually read it cover to cover, which is not as common as I'd like to admit.
I tend to get sort of halfway through and then some other book jumps out, right?
And it's a beautiful little book.
It includes several of the standard teachings that we are studying in *The Heart of Buddha's Teaching*.
But it also includes a really touching personal tale.
As a young monk in Vietnam, Thich Nhat Hanh, like most other young people, fell in love, with this nun.
Of course, they were both in the order, a celibate order, so they couldn't act on it.
But they were tempted.
He admits this.
It's kind of beautiful, very vulnerable.
The spoilers: they never did act on it.
And it has a sad ending.
Actually, he lost touch with her and couldn't find out where she'd ended up.
Of course, it was in a country at war, so it's not too surprising.

And so when it became clear that Desiree would be a great choice for the next Shuso, and I knew she had this history with Thich Nhat Hanh and his teachings, I thought, oh, maybe she could teach this book with us.
But in her conversations with Ryushin, a wider plan emerged, which is wonderful, too.
And so we ended up with *The Heart of Buddhist Teachings*.
But it's a little bit of a copy-pasted book, actually.
Yeah, they added stuff to make it all go together.
But the exact same two chapters about the three marks of existence and the three doors of liberation are in this book, pretty much word for word, as far as I can tell.
They have great material to work with, so Thich Nhat Hanh taught so much.
He must have had a lot of devoted students constantly recording and transcribing.
And I'm sure he wrote [unclear: "row two"] as well.
So enough material for well over 100 books in English.
Maybe it's closer to 200 by now.
And they'll probably keep coming out, like him dying doesn't have to slow that down.
It's amazing.
So prolific.
And then all that came to be.
And we're in our class with Desiree leading us on a tour through the Eightfold Path to the chapters before the ones that had caught my interest.
And Mary interested me by holding up on the screen the other day this book, *The Eightfold Path*, edited by Jikyo Wolfer, which I hadn't noticed.
I just missed it in Desiree's recommendations.
Or maybe Mary found it some other way.
I don't know.

She's like a dharma sister to Joan Stam, who's often here.
Also studied with Edo.
And I knew that Jikyo and Edo had created this little press called Temple Ground Press.
Not a long catalog, but five or six books or something.
And they're all very similar.
There's a theme and an introduction.
And then they invite women teachers to write chapters.
And so I got a hold of it right away.
I'm like, wow, cool.

I hope so.
But it made me remember that when they first started that press, somewhere around 2014 or 12 or something, I was at a Soto Zen Buddhist Association meeting that both of them were at, Jikyo and Edo.
And they set up a little table to talk about this.
And on their table, they were giving away books.
So that was easy to get interested in.
And so I received this book called *Seeds of Virtue, Seeds of Change*.
And it too sat on the shelf, untouched.
So last night, some combination of something or other in the email led me to this book.
And this initial one didn't have a particular theme.
Subsequent ones have a theme like the Eightfold Path or Dogen's teachings or teachings in difficult times or something.
The blurb on the back of this one just says: "For the first time, 27 Soto Zen women priests come together to offer teachings in response to a call for spiritual insight and balance.
This collection opens possibilities of deeper awareness for cultivating compassion during troubled times."
A lot of their motivation, of course, was to make the teachings of women more obvious.
And one of the things I appreciated later when I thought about it is the subtitle is "A Collection of Zen Teachings."
It's nice they didn't say "a collection of Zen women's teachings," like you have to be paying attention.
And if it was a usual collection, like all men or almost all men, it wouldn't say "a collection of male teachings," right?
It wouldn't say that.
So that's kind of brilliant on their part.
So I skimmed and speed read and jumped around a bunch.
I spent the evening on this. [unclear: "Razor's away"].
So I'm doing whatever I feel like.
And one of them really jumped out at me.
So I want to share with you the beginning of the essay by Itsudo Patty Krall.
Patty is a part of a Dharma couple, Patty and Herald.
And they are the founders of the Ashland Zen Center in Ashland, Oregon.
Our Dharma friends, Jeffrey and Laura Vogel, lived there for a while and practiced with them.
And the teacher below them is a woman named Ramana Wehmeyer.
And I was at Tassajara with Ramona.
I really love her.
So I feel connected to them.
And I won't say too much about Patty.
I'll let her speak for herself.
This will all circle back in the end to where it started somehow.
So here's her essay.
It was just a wide open topic from the editor: write anything you want.
And it seems like that was challenging for Patty.
So the piece is called "Notes from the Frontier, June 26, 2013."
*Eido knocked on the door today via email and asked me to write an essay for Temple Ground Press's new book, giving voice to women teachers, known and unknown.
I fall into the latter category and I'm happy to be there.*
Known and unknown, latter category.
*At first I balked.
Siskiyo-sansui-do, aka Ashland Zen Center, is just a small Zen center in an old yellow house and barn in a small college town lost in the Siskiyo Mountains of southern Oregon.
I am lost too and I have no need to be found.
But she who must be obeyed chimed in, quote, "Summer in the Rogue Valley of southern Oregon, a time for work practice, painting, gardening, canning, writing.
And there's no shortage of Zen authors out there.
Why do they need this nobody's voice?"*
So I guess she who must be obeyed is her ego.
*And actually I teach most often by contact rather than with words.
The mountains and rivers, the blueberries and tomato worms, those are the things that inform me.
I share them with my students and they share themselves with me.
Winter we sew Buddha's robes and study around the fire, fill the frozen bird feeders and sit zazen together.
Spring we cut peonies for the altar, plant berry starts, weed and sit zazen together.*
*Summer we paint the tool shed, string cable for the deer fence, put up our tea booth in the park for Fourth of July and we sit zazen together.

Autumn we harvest bushels of apples, fill the pantry with quarts of applesauce, walk the Rogue River trail bearing witness to fall's brilliant display, stock the woodshed with dry bark and kindling and sit zazen together.
We turn compost and sit zazen together.
We repair the irrigation system and sit zazen together.
We clean the zendo and sit together.*
*We rake mountains of sycamore and cottonwood leaves and sit together.
We chant the Buddhas and ancestors and we sit together.
We screen the crawl space to keep the skunks out and we sit together.
What else is there?
For years I have taught the Dharma through body, simple and straightforward.
Like the Chinese Zen master who wrote more than a thousand years ago, "Magical power, marvelous action, chopping wood, carrying water."
I'm not sure what I can offer to the greater circle when there are such accomplished teachers on Dogen, Nagarjuna and the Lotus Sutra.
But good teachers are skillful, they sneak up on you from the side, widening your field of vision and readying your mind.*

*Quote, "Such a book will help to encourage teachers towards their own publication for the sake of their sanghas, provide an historical record of Dharma teachings for our times, lead students to connect with teachers with whom they might wish to practice, and influence newcomers to the Dharma.
And it's helpful for those who are not in the proximity of teachers or centers."*
*Eido's invitation reads, "turning words for the sake of their sanghas and helpful for those who are not in proximity to teachers and centers."
Beyond the gates of the large residential training centers, traditional Zen practice of chopping wood and carrying water isn't sexy, or even particularly popular.
People are more interested in talks, cyber sanghas and retreats, and really interesting and inspiring teachers.
Isolated in the mountains without a dazzling array of workshops or visiting circuit teachers, our group remains small.
Small is good, small is intimate.
But our sangha is aging and could use new blood.*
Skip a little bit and then one more part.
So she's still thinking about whether to write this essay a month later, right?
*August 19th.
Weeks of painting behind us, I treat myself one morning to a Starbucks.
So have many others and I take my place in the long line.
Several of the locals are visiting with one another as they wait and I feel a tap on my shoulder.
Turning around I see a familiar woman, a face of a woman who is active in our local peace house.
She says, "I know you haven't seen me for a while at the Zendo.
It occurs to me you might wonder why people come and sit for a while and one day you don't see them again.*
*Would you like to know why I quit coming?"
I greet her and assure her yes, I would be happy to know this.
"Well," she says, "I really like to come and meditate in the morning with the others, even though I'm not really crazy about your traditional forms and all.
But I was willing to overlook that.
Then one morning as I was last to leave and you and Harold were putting all the cushions away, you asked me if I would like to help you put things away too.
I'm a busy person with a job and a family.
I come to the Zendo to find peace and quiet, not to do more work.
I just don't need more people wanting something from me.
I hope you understand."
I thanked her for sharing her feelings, but before we could talk further the barista asked for my order, one plain bagel, hold the cream cheese and a black decaf coffee,*
*Make mine full bodied please.
And I turned to invite her to sit with me to discuss further, but she had ordered hers to go and was already gone.
This is not a new experience for me.
Our group is small and wholehearted.
It is a seedling of 20 years of practice here in a community of 20,000 people.
Will it survive along the way?
Even thrive?
Don't know.
Doesn't matter.*
And then she goes on, going through the rest of her summer and still thinking about whether to write this article or not write this article, and of course she's writing it all along.
It's quite a wonderful little adventure in her mind.
Maybe that's why I related to it.
The other articles are very concise and clear, and this one was a ramble through Itsudo Patty's mind, and I liked her a lot when I met her.
So what is the Dharma anyway?
And what are these complex teachings that Thich Nhat Hanh does a lovely job making accessible, but he doesn't beat around the bush either, right?
He brings up some challenging and interesting teachings in our studies.
And even the ones that seem really straightforward, like Right Livelihood or something like that, turn out to be quite deep.
But now here in the last chapters that we're going to study in our wonderful class with Desiree, we're right back to what inspired me in the first place, the Three Doors of Liberation.
It struck me that in her humble and reluctant maybe passage, Paddy's writing is actually a wonderful expression of these three doors.
So I want to see if I can offer some connections here.
The Three Doors of Liberation are called Emptiness, Signlessness, and Wishlessness.
Here we're into the powerful wisdom teachings that emerged more strongly later in Buddhism with the great arising of the Mahayana, the Great Way, of which Zen is a part.
The terms behind these teachings are mentioned in the Pali Canon.
I looked it up.
I didn't think they were, but they're mentioned.
They're in the early teachings for sure, but as far as I can tell they're just briefly in there, not a central point.
They show up as much more central and much more elaborated as Buddhism went along and evolved and changed, which is interesting all in itself.
We have this kind of, I don't know, originalist bias: is this the real Buddhism?
Actually, it's more a conversation than a thing, I think, ever changing.
It has evolved and will continue to evolve.
And Thich Nhat Hanh with us is doing some interesting selecting too, like which things feel to him important and which things don't.
He's quite bold, actually, Thich Nhat Hanh.
I don't know if you've noticed that.
It's like, this is not true Buddhism.
Maybe he's right.
Yeah, I don't know.
Each teacher is doing that, whether they know it or not.
So at least he was very straightforward with us.
But these three are like signposts that point to this bigger vision, beyond just being a little less stressed out or a little calmer, to the transformational vision of practice.

I was in a dialogue the other day with some colleagues, and what emerged is an interesting idea that practice has two interlocking processes that we might call the path of healing and the path of transformation, or maybe path of liberation, and that both are important.
Healing's easier to make sense of, right?
We're sick.
We want to feel better.
We're stressed.
We want to be grounded.
We're projecting on somebody and it's making us crazy, and we would like to be free of that and see their goodness and reconnect and find love again.
So this is the path of healing, and it's wonderful.
Practice offers us tools for healing that we never would have known about.
These teachings are more strongly in the path of liberation and transformation.
What if all of what I just said wasn't exactly what was going on anyway?
It's a deeper dimension.
And it's pointed to by the two truths that Desirai mentioned last week, the relative and the ultimate; there are lots of different ways these are talked about.
The ordinary world we can think about and see and try to improve, wonderful.
We should do that.
And then there's the sense of the world that's beyond anything that we can ever see or improve or even understand, more like a feeling.
So these terms and these practices point to our life beyond the life that we can talk about, beyond the life that we can put into concepts.
It's all very hard to talk about.
Words can only point in the right direction.
It's like the famous finger pointing to the moon.
So let's see if I can unpack these a little bit, and hopefully that'll inform a little bit how you read Thich Nhat Hanh as well.
Emptiness, the first of the three, we talk about this more.
This means not that things are bad or voided out or dark or [unclear: "militations"].
My computer might have frozen there for a minute.
Did my voice come through?
Okay, good.
It's just my visual, I guess.
Okay, good.
So emptiness all by itself is very confusing.
It's empty of what?
Empty of boundaries, empty of limits.
We may believe in all this, and it's not very believable that I believe I'm separate from you.
As I prepared this talk, I believed that my butt was separate from my couch, or that my being alive is separate from my sooner or later being dead.
It all seems like very separate, different things: different objects, different experiences, different processes, different stuff.
But in this teaching, it's a recognition that that's just an idea.
It's a very powerful idea.
Our mind can gather a lot of evidence in support of these ideas of separation, but it's not really how it is.
The reason why there's three of them is that in this teaching, we need more than just this idea of emptiness to get this.
We need more markers and signposts to help us keep going in the right direction, because emptiness all by itself is very like, well, then where do I go?
You go nowhere.
What?
Like my famous quotation in the Prajnaparamita literature, which is really an explication of all of this.
That's when it really took hold.
They talk about the students always being in dialogue with a teacher, usually one student in dialogue with Buddha.
And so Subhuti asked the Buddha, well, if the Buddhas have nowhere to stand, where do they stand?
And the Buddha says, exactly, Subhuti.
They stand in having nowhere to stand.
Isn't that wonderful?
But what do you do with it?
What do you do with it?
The second two of these three doors, three pointers to a bigger life, are signlessness and wishlessness.
And here the English is very problematic.
Probably the original language wasn't much better.
Signlessness in Sanskrit is anumita.
So anumita is a sign.
And Thay talks about this.
A sign is some experience that you map onto something.
A sign is evidence.
So a sight is a sign.
A sound is a sign.
A thought is a sign.
A concept is a sign.
An idea is a sign.
And the idea is that we then confuse the signs as pointing to a very solid, fixed, dividable, conceptualizable reality, right?
So the signs point us to misunderstand emptiness.
But we can't actually notice emptiness particularly.
What we notice are these signs.
Our life is just awash in signs.
We're immersed in signs, millions of signs per day probably.
So that's nimitta, signs.
This term is anumita, and ah is just a negation.
It means not.
So to understand not signs, or not sign-ness, or the experience of the signs as not being what you think they are.
It's awkward to translate.
Signlessness is okay, but what it really means is that what you're perceiving as signs are not what you think they are.
It's not that there are no signs.
There's tons of signs, an overwhelming array of signs.
And our signs are what we think to be real.
So emptiness and signlessness are pointers towards another dimension of experience that we don't always notice.
We feel it sometimes, but often we lose track of it.
There seems to be a very strong correlation between suffering and stress and our ability to actually feel this aspect of reality.
The more stress, the less we feel any of this.
We're really lost in the conditioned world when we're stressed out.
So the question here is how do I practice with all this?
And what do I do with this information?
I think it can be interesting.
You could go get a PhD in Buddhist philosophy.
No question.
People do.
But how do I practice with this?
That's where the third of the three doors comes in: wishlessness.
Thich Nhat Hanh actually chose the English word aimlessness.
I think that has all kinds of connotations that are confusing.
Wishlessness is much more common, and in my humble opinion that's a little more helpful.
But still, it's just words.
Just signs.
Because here again, we have a negation built in, the lessness.
In English we put lessness at the end, and in Sanskrit we put this negation at the front, which makes more sense.
So here, I'm going to scan Sanskrit.
Sanskrit is a pranahita.
A pranahita.
So there's that a again.
And then we have pranahita.
Pranahita means to reach for something.
It's an ordinary word in Sanskrit, to reach for something.
And so here it's about how we interact with reality.
We reach for it, right?
Conceptually, physically, in every way, we reach for stuff.
We want to hold on to it.
We want to know it.
We want to bring it closer so we can take a look at it.
We want to take a look so we can answer our most important fundamental question about everything when we're in this realm: do I like this or not?
When we reach for it and we realize it's an object of desire, we want to hold on to it.
We reach for it and realize it's an object of aversion, we want to push it away, which is another kind of reaching.
Get away.
I don't want you.
And so we get caught in this fundamental habit of pranahita, of reaching for things.
So a-pranahita means not reaching for things.
It's releasing from this powerful, deep conditioning.
The reason is not that there's exactly anything wrong with reaching for things, but our constant tendency to do this hooks into everything else and holds us in this limited, small frame.
So that's what I love so much about Patti's writing.
She's invited to reach for something, to write an essay and be published.
And maybe she has a little trouble with pushing it away at first.
But then it's so beautiful, and I wish I had time to read the whole essay.

Then she recognizes herself as a teacher, in a beautiful passage about going through the seasons, experiencing the things that need to be experienced, being with what is, together with sangha, and sitting zazen with it, season after season, day after day, year after year.
So this is Zen as life, right?
Zen as a lived practice.
I especially love that she includes that little incident in the coffee shop.
Maybe that was just because I could put myself in her shoes so readily, because that's happened to me many times as well.
A little bit less likely, maybe, because Bellingham's getting big.
But many, many times I've run into somebody when I was just trying to hang out and do my thing, who wanted to bend my ear and tell me about why they feel guilty for not coming to the sangha.
Or, in the case of her person, defend why they weren't coming to the sangha.
That happens less often, sometimes.
And I just love her practice of emptiness there.
It's a really deep response that she has.
First, she's unguarded and undefended, and she's willing to listen and interested to discuss further.
She was going to let go of her solo coffee break.
That's pretty good.
If I was her, I'd be like, I'm just here to have my coffee, man.

She's ready to let that go and sit down with this woman who's giving her this correction, that because of Patti's behavior she would no longer come to the zendo, asking her to help put away the cushions.
What a big burden.
And then when the person's gone, she accepts that too.
I turned, and she was already gone.
So that's the Heart Sutra's mantra right there.
*Gathe gathe par gathe.
Par sam gathe.

Bodhisattva.* And she doesn't know whether this way of being together, this way of sitting with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, will thrive in this little college town in 21st century America, as unexciting as it is, or not.
She says, don't know.
Doesn't matter.
Doesn't matter.
So "doesn't matter" is exactly the practice of wishlessness.
It includes the healthy wish for all beings to be happy, for sure, but with us standing in the ground of letting it all go, right?
Standing in the ground of letting it all go.
So maybe we always practice that way together.
And it's exciting and fun for me.
I do enjoy going to meetings and talking to people and saying, oh, yeah, we're growing.
We're doing well.
We're offering all these things.
Sure, there's occasional problems, blah, blah, blah.
Sure, we all make mistakes.
I make mistakes, blah, blah, blah.
But I have this feeling, which I have talked about and [unclear: "reinforced of wish here"], right?
Of reaching for.
*Oh,* Red Cedar Zen is going to survive.
We've got a building.
We're growing.
Think how much we'll grow when we get there.
It's going to be so exciting.
Thinking about structures so we'll stay more connected as we get big.
Become a giant congregation.
Eventually, you won't know any of the members.
There'll just be thousands of them, right?
People sitting zazen everywhere.
But we don't know.
And in a real deep, fundamental way, she's right.
She's really right.
It doesn't matter.
And then I was thinking about signlessness some more, and recognizing that actually the way to study signlessness is to study the signs, to really become intimate with everything.
And we can only do that through signs.
So at this point I moved downstairs to have some breakfast with my pile of books and my laptop.
And I ran into another book, which was sitting out on the table: *Northwest Trees*.
Lately, as I'm sure I've mentioned, I'm reconnecting a bit more with the early adult love of nature.
And not just nature as an experience and an immersion, but the details of nature, the biology and natural history and ecology of nature.
I have an undergraduate degree in this too, but I lost track of it.
Life got in the way.
It's like my first love, and I lost track of her.
So I'm falling back in love with Mother Earth in this more detailed way.
This book, *Northwest Trees*, I think I bought pretty soon after we moved to Bellingham.
The first couple of chapters seem familiar, but from there, not so familiar.
So I think it sat on my shelf for 30 years.
And it's a beautiful, beautiful book.
Every chapter is an in-depth exploration of each of our Northwest native trees: how to identify them, where they grow, what they look like, the details of their biology, how many cones and seeds.
Seeds are mostly very light, thousands and thousands of seeds per pound because they can fly through the air.
But they're not all the same.
Some of these conifers have lighter seeds than others, and they can fly further.
They know all the science of this.
And then there are the beautiful hand-made science illustrations of every tree, with details so you can recognize it.
And not just that, but the story of these trees: how they seem to function in ecosystems, what they can do and what they can't do, and how they interact with the other trees in the forest over time.
And it's over long scales of time, right?
Hundreds of years, thousands of years.
It's a very grounding pile of science towards the deep ecology of the forest.
Some of this I knew, of course, and much I'm learning more or remembering.
I'm trying to read a chapter a morning after breakfast.
Some days I remember.
Some of it was really familiar.

For instance, I know that Douglas fir, which isn't really a fir botanically, but it's what got called that by the early botanist, is more drought tolerant than many of the other northwest native trees, like the western hemlock.
And it's faster growing, whereas the western hemlock, most of the time, is slower growing.
Especially because the western hemlock is much, much, much more shade tolerant.
And you may know all this too.
So in the increasing dimness of a mature forest, western hemlock's little seeds can germinate and its little trees can just grow very slowly in the shade, kind of waiting for their chance.
But in a new clearing from forest fire or a clear cut, Douglas fir moves in much more quickly.
It grows faster.
It can handle the dry conditions of this disrupted environment.
And it creates good conditions for the baby western hemlocks.
Then when the great big mature Douglas fir falls down, it creates this big opening of light.
And those western hemlocks that have been on low gear for decades maybe go, okay, we're ready.
And then a mature western hemlock will, pretty inevitably, replace the fallen Douglas fir.
Unless there's a new disruption and the system starts over again, right?
So it was wonderful being reminded of these dynamics and learning a lot more about things I didn't know.
I've never been quite clear on Pacific silver firs, which one they are exactly and where they fit into this mosaic, and how you tell them from the...
Anyway, I'm really having a good time.
For years now I go backpacking almost every summer, and then I run into the limits of my knowledge every year.
I'm like, dang it.
I never did look that up.
Okay, next year I'm going to look that up.
So I'm looking that up.
It's wonderful.
It's exciting.
